questions.subject: Pre-vocational Studies
questions.topic: Meaning, importance and scope of Agriculture
questions.subtopic: Agriculture as production and related activity
questions.learningObjective: Explain agriculture through selected plant/animal production examples, distinguishing scale from the nature of the activity.
questions.prompt: Explain agriculture using one crop example and one animal example. Show what people do in each example.
questions.answer: Agriculture includes growing plants and raising animals for useful products. For example, growers plant and care for okra, while poultry keepers raise chickens for products such as eggs.
questions.explanation: A suitable explanation includes purposeful production rather than only naming something eaten.

markingGuide.description: Explains the production/growing/raising idea.
Gives an appropriate crop activity.
Gives an appropriate animal activity.

questions.topic: Meaning, importance and scope of Agriculture
questions.subtopic: Agriculture as production and related activity
questions.learningObjective: Explain agriculture through selected plant/animal production examples, distinguishing scale from the nature of the activity.
questions.prompt: A learner says that growing vegetables in a small backyard cannot be agriculture because the plot is not a large commercial farm. Explain the mistake.
questions.answer: Agriculture is not defined only by a large plot or commercial scale. Purposefully growing vegetables is crop production even in a small backyard.
questions.explanation: Size can change how production is organised; it does not by itself remove the activity from agriculture.

markingGuide.description: Rejects large scale as a necessary condition.

questions.learningObjective: Explain selected contributions of agriculture to food, raw materials and livelihoods without promising that any enterprise always succeeds.

questions.subject: Pre-vocational Studies
questions.topic: Meaning, importance and scope of Agriculture
questions.learningObjective: Explain selected contributions of agriculture to food, raw materials and livelihoods without promising that any enterprise always succeeds.
questions.prompt: A fictional community has a large vegetable harvest, but transport to buyers is interrupted. Does a large harvest alone guarantee that every household can obtain the vegetables? Explain one reason and one role that delivery or marketing can play.
questions.answer: No. Producing vegetables does not by itself ensure they reach people or that every household can obtain them. Delivery and marketing can help connect available produce with users.
questions.explanation: This deepens the importance-of-agriculture task by distinguishing production from access. It does not predict prices, diagnose nutrition or claim that one delivery action guarantees food security.

markingGuide.description: Rejects production alone as a guarantee of household access, with a relevant reason.

questions.subject: Pre-vocational Studies
questions.subtopic: Soil as a natural growth medium
questions.learningObjective: Explain soil as a natural medium containing mineral/organic solids, water and air, rather than only loose dirt or fixed proportions.
questions.prompt: Give a simple meaning of soil that includes its role for land plants and more than one kind of material it contains.
questions.answer: Soil is a natural material near the land surface that can support rooted plants. It includes mineral and organic material, with water and air in spaces between the solids.
questions.explanation: This age-appropriate account avoids fixed component percentages or a claim that every soil has an identical mixture.

markingGuide.description: Explains the natural growth-medium idea.
Includes appropriate solids such as mineral/organic material.
Includes water or air as part of the soil system.

questions.learningObjective: Compare broad sandy/clayey descriptions and recognise that colour alone does not establish loam; this is written reasoning, not actual sample identification.

questions.learningObjective: Compare broad sandy/clayey descriptions and recognise that colour alone does not establish loam; this is written reasoning, not actual sample identification.
questions.prompt: A fictional soil card says, This soil is dark, so its texture must be loam. Explain why colour alone is insufficient, and name the particle groups relevant to texture.
questions.answer: Texture concerns the relative amounts of sand, silt and clay, not colour alone. More texture evidence is needed before a loam classification is justified.
questions.explanation: The source’s three classroom labels are a selected simplification, not all scientific texture classes. No percentages or universal best-soil claim is assessed.

markingGuide.description: Rejects colour alone as sufficient texture evidence.
Names sand, silt and clay as the relevant particle groups.

questions.learningObjective: Explain soil fertility/infertility in relation to adequate nutrient supply for specified plants, keeping other growth conditions and need for evidence explicit.
questions.prompt: Explain low soil fertility in terms of the needs of a specified crop, rather than simply calling the soil bad.
questions.answer: Low fertility means the soil does not supply the needed plant nutrients in adequate amounts or balance for that crop. The explanation should relate to nutrient supply and the crop’s needs.
questions.explanation: Fertility is one aspect of growing conditions, not a diagnosis that every difficulty is caused by nutrients.

markingGuide.description: Links fertility to plant nutrient supply.

questions.learningObjective: Explain soil fertility/infertility in relation to adequate nutrient supply for specified plants, keeping other growth conditions and need for evidence explicit.

questions.subtopic: Home Economics as applied resource use
